conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your scheduled hernia repair, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been having a lot of pain near my old incision, and they said the hernia was starting to block things a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the imaging showed part of your colon was partially stuck in the hernia. We were able to reduce it, but because the defect is large, surgery is the best option to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will you be using mesh? I remember last time they did the Puestow, it was a big surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll be doing a primary repair with Prolene mesh overlay. It helps strengthen the area and reduces the chance of the hernia coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how long will I be out after the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay in the hospital for a few days. We’ll start you on IV fluids and pain medication, and gradually get you back on food once your bowels start working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gastroparesis before—will that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your history. We’ll start you on clear liquids on post-op day one and advance slowly. We’ll also continue your pancreatic enzymes and monitor how you tolerate things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes—should I take my metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll hold metformin while you’re not eating and switch to insulin if needed. We’ll restart it once you’re on a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. What about my other meds—like for my mood and nerves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll resume most of your psychiatric medications as soon as you’re able to take pills. The team will coordinate with psychiatry to make sure nothing is missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some PTSD flare-ups lately—work stuff, old memories. I hope I can sleep okay here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help with that. You’re on prazosin and zolpidem at home—we’ll restart those as appropriate. Let the nurses know if you’re having trouble resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went very well—ventral hernia repair with mesh, no complications. You’re in the recovery unit now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks… I feel groggy. Is the drain in my side normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we placed a JP drain in your right lower quadrant to collect any fluid and prevent buildup. It will stay in until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s temporary. We’ll remove it tonight or tomorrow morning once you’re up and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s okay right now. I see the PCA button—should I use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it as needed. It’s hydromorphone, and it’s safe when used properly. We’ll switch to oral meds once you start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Glucose was 154 this morning—well controlled. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try some water or ice chips today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds—will I still get the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for now, but once you’re on oral pain meds, we’ll discontinue it. Chronic pain service reviewed your case and recommended continuing gabapentin and adding acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds—can you tell me which ones I’ll restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart most: lisinopril, simvastatin, omeprazole, amitriptyline, ziprasidone, duloxetine, gabapentin, metformin once you’re eating, and your pancreatic enzymes with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool softener? I don’t want to strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you docusate twice a day and senna at night to help. Avoid heavy lifting for at least six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is about a 3. I had some broth and jello—no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll upgrade you to a soft diet tomorrow—maybe mashed potatoes, applesauce. And we removed the catheter this morning—you voided fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no problem. The drain is a little annoying, but I’ll manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re tolerating food well. We’re advancing you to a regular diet. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4, but manageable. I’m on oral meds now—hydromorphone as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and acetaminophen regularly. We discontinued the PCA. You’re walking well—great job with the ambulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I get discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well today, we’re planning for tomorrow morning. You need to tolerate a regular diet, be pain-controlled, and have no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be going home with the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll stay in until your follow-up. You’ll need to empty it daily, keep the site clean, and watch for signs of infection—increased redness, fever, or cloudy drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take Keflex four times a day for 14 days to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well—afebrile, eating, walking, pain controlled. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll be removed at your follow-up. You can shower—just pat the area dry. No baths or swimming until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over 10 pounds, no driving while on pain meds. Continue walking daily. Follow up with surgery and your PCP in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand. I’ll take my meds, care for the drain, and call if anything’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll see you in clinic to remove the staples and drain. Take care.
